note: Samuel, Saul and David's rise, indexed selectively: the passages that anchor formation have been drawn out of the narrative, and the coverage note records what was left. Not cited by the curriculum or the Scriptural Appendix.
prediction_note: Forecast: 16:7 the anchor for C07; 24 and 26 for PR06; Jonathan for PR26. Outcome: as forecast. Unforecast: 25:23-31 (Abigail) is the most exact narrative of PR09 anywhere in the index — the objective changed, one thing conceded early — and Nabal and David together give a two-sided PR22 counter-example; 1:12-17 (Eli and Hannah) is a precise PR16 counter-example; 23:16 anchors PR21.
coverage_note: Indexed selectively. Not indexed: the ark among the Philistines and its return (4-7); Saul's anointing and early reign (9-11, 13-14), except as referenced; the command against Amalek (15:1-12), which belongs to the herem texts the index does not anchor — 15:13-31 is indexed only for how Saul answers for his disobedience; the battle narrative of 17 beyond David's speech; David in Saul's court and his flight (19, 20:1-29, 21-22, 23:1-14, 23:19-29); chapter 26, which repeats the pattern of 24; David among the Philistines and the raids (27, 29-30:20); the medium at Endor (28); the battle at Gilboa (31:1-7).

entries.pericope: I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit… I poured out my soul before Yahweh… Eli thought she had been drunken
entries.connection: Hannah, childless, provoked 'year by year' by her husband's other wife, weeping and not eating. Her husband's comfort misses the mark: 'Am I not better to you than ten sons?' She goes to pray. 'She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed to Yahweh, and wept bitterly… Hannah spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard.' Sacred Lament in its interior form: 'I poured out my soul before Yahweh… I have been speaking out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation.' C09's secret place, kept even in a crowded sanctuary. And the cost of judging too quickly: 'Eli thought she had been drunken. Eli said to her, "How long will you be drunken? Put away your wine from you."' Listening as Mercy holds that full attention 'very often uncovers a hidden reality or an invisible pain that would have made your correction unnecessary'; Eli corrects first and listens second, and to his credit, once he hears, he blesses: 'Go in peace.' 'Her facial expression wasn't sad any more.' C19.

entries.pericope: He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes… Talk no more so exceeding proudly
entries.connection: Hannah's song, which Mary's Magnificat echoes (Luke 1:46-55). 'Talk no more so exceeding proudly. Don't let arrogance come out of your mouth, For Yahweh is a God of knowledge. By him actions are weighed.' C22. Then the reversals: 'The bows of the mighty men are broken. Those who stumbled are armed with strength. Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread. Those who were hungry are satisfied… He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes.' C16's downward-and-upward order of God's action. As at Luke 1:46-55, no practice is tagged.

entries.pericope: The sons of Eli were base men; they didn't know Yahweh… his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn't restrain them… 'Speak; for your servant hears.'
entries.connection: Two households in the sanctuary. Eli's sons take the offerings by force — 'you shall give it to me now; and if not, I will take it by force' — and abuse the women who served at the tent; Eli rebukes them mildly and does nothing more, and the verdict falls on him too: 'his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn't restrain them.' C08's corrupt priesthood and C14's failure of a father's responsibility. Beside them a boy sleeping near the ark, called three times in the night. Eli, to his lasting credit, recognises what is happening and teaches the boy to listen: 'if he calls you, that you shall say, "Speak, Yahweh; for your servant hears."' C09's posture of prayer in one sentence. The message is against Eli; the boy 'feared to show Eli the vision,' and tells him 'every bit, and hid nothing from him' — C08's true prophet at the start. Eli's answer is C22's: 'It is Yahweh. Let him do what seems good to him.'

entries.pericope: Make us a king to judge us like all the nations… they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me… that we also may be like all the nations
entries.connection: 'Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.' Samuel takes it personally and prays; God reframes it: 'they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not be king over them.' Samuel describes what a king will cost — 'He will take your sons… He will take your daughters… He will take your fields… and you shall be his servants' — and the people answer: 'No; but we will have a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations.' The Citizen-Stranger asks, 'Where have I assimilated without noticing?' This is assimilation chosen with eyes open (medium). C17 and C18.

entries.pericope: Here I am. Witness against me… Whose ox have I taken?… far be it from me that I should sin against Yahweh in ceasing to pray for you
entries.connection: At the end of his public life Samuel submits to an audit in front of the nation: 'Here I am. Witness against me before Yahweh, and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Of whose hand have I taken a ransom to blind my eyes therewith? I will restore it to you.' The Moral Audit's money and partiality areas, examined in public with a promise of restitution, and passed: 'You have not defrauded us.' C04 and C08. Then the people who rejected his leadership ask him to pray for them, and he does not hold it against them: 'far be it from me that I should sin against Yahweh in ceasing to pray for you: but I will instruct you in the good and the right way.' Shedding Harshness in a leader who has just been set aside (medium). C27.

entries.pericope: To obey is better than sacrifice… 'I have sinned… because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice'… 'I have sinned: yet please honor me now before the elders of my people'
entries.connection: The command Saul was given in this chapter belongs to the herem texts the index does not anchor (see the coverage note); what the index anchors is how Saul answers for disobeying it. He greets Samuel with a claim — 'I have performed the commandment of Yahweh' — over the sound of the livestock he kept. Then he blames others ('the people spared the best'), then re-labels ('to sacrifice to Yahweh your God'), then repeats the claim. Samuel's answer is C06's principle: 'Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.' Saul's confession, when it comes, still carries an excuse — 'because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice' — and a request: 'I have sinned: yet please honor me now before the elders of my people.' The Failure Recovery Protocol's counter-example: the failure named, but with explanatory context and a concern for face (medium). C21's anatomy of a man governed by the crowd, and C08.

entries.pericope: Man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart… There remains yet the youngest, and behold, he is keeping the sheep
entries.connection: 'How long will you mourn for Saul?' Samuel is sent to Bethlehem and, seeing Jesse's eldest, assumes he has found the king. 'But Yahweh said to Samuel, "Don't look on his face, or on the height of his stature; because I have rejected him: for I see not as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart."' C07's lens corrected, and C06's seeing beneath the surface. Seven sons pass by. 'Are all your children here?' 'There remains yet the youngest, and behold, he is keeping the sheep.' The one not even invited is chosen — C13's ordinary work as the place God looks.

entries.pericope: I can't go with these; for I have not tested them… You come to me with a sword… but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies… the battle is Yahweh's
entries.connection: David's qualifications are a shepherd's: 'when a lion or a bear came, and took a lamb out of the flock, I went out after him… Yahweh who delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me.' C13's ordinary faithfulness as the training for the extraordinary moment, and C05's apprenticeship in a field no one watched. Offered the king's armour, he refuses what he has not practised with: 'I can't go with these; for I have not tested them.' Then C22's ground: 'You come to me with a sword, and with a spear… but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies… that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn't save with sword and spear: for the battle is Yahweh's.'

entries.pericope: The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David… Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him, and gave it to David, and his clothing, even to his sword, and to his bow
entries.connection: 'The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul… Then Jonathan and David made a covenant.' The heir to the throne gives the shepherd boy his robe, his armour, his sword and his bow — the symbols of his own succession. C22's humility in the person with the most to lose, and C13's friendship as covenant.

entries.pericope: Saul has slain his thousands, David his ten thousands… Saul was very angry… 'What can he have more but the kingdom?' Saul eyed David from that day and forward
entries.connection: A victory song sung by the women of Israel, and one line in it: 'Saul has slain his thousands, David his ten thousands.' 'Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him… "What can he have more but the kingdom?" Saul eyed David from that day and forward.' C21's anatomy of envy, beginning with a comparison and ending, the next day, with a spear. The Discipline of Gradualism warns that comparison is 'a category error' (medium as counter-example); here it is the gate through which the evil spirit enters. C20.

entries.pericope: Why should he be put to death? What has he done?… Saul cast his spear at him to strike him… They kissed one another, and wept one with another, and David wept the most
entries.connection: Saul tells Jonathan plainly what David's survival costs him: 'For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, you shall not be established, nor your kingdom.' Jonathan's answer is a question of justice — 'Why should he be put to death? What has he done?' — and his father throws a spear at him. Jonathan warns David with the arrows, and they part: 'They kissed one another, and wept one with another, and David wept the most.' Unobligated Loyalty at its most costly: fidelity to a friend in danger against the interests of his own inheritance and the wishes of his own father, with nothing to gain (medium). C13 and C16.

entries.pericope: Jonathan, Saul's son, arose, and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God. He said to him, 'Don't be afraid'
entries.connection: David is a fugitive in the wilderness with Saul hunting him. 'Jonathan, Saul's son, arose, and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God. He said to him, "Don't be afraid; for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you; and you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you."' Verbal Almsgiving exactly: seeking out the discouraged and isolated and offering a good word as a genuine act of charity — at personal risk, and conceding the throne in the same sentence. C13's friendship, and C19's hope given by one person to another.

entries.pericope: David's heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt… May Yahweh judge between me and you… but my hand shall not be on you… 'You are more righteous than I'
entries.connection: The man hunting him walks alone into the cave where David is hiding. His men call it providence: 'Behold, the day of which Yahweh said to you, "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand."' David cuts off the corner of Saul's robe — 'It happened afterward, that David's heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt.' Watchfulness at its finest grain: conscience troubled by the small act before it could become the large one (medium). He holds back his men, then calls after the king and shows him the cloth: 'May Yahweh judge between me and you, and may Yahweh avenge me of you; but my hand shall not be on you.' Non-Retaliation with the enemy defenceless, and vengeance explicitly left to God. C03. Saul weeps: 'You are more righteous than I; for you have done good to me, whereas I have done evil to you.' C15. Chapter 26 repeats the pattern and is not indexed separately.

entries.pericope: On me, my lord, on me be the iniquity; and please let your handmaid speak… Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, that have kept me this day from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand
entries.connection: David's men had protected a rich man's shepherds in the wilderness — 'They were a wall to us both by night and by day' — and David asks for a share at shearing time. Nabal refuses with contempt: 'Who is David?… Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my meat… and give it to men who I don't know where they come from?' The helper repaid with insult. David's reaction fails Unreciprocated Care's question — 'Do I only serve those who thank me?' — with four hundred swords: 'He has returned me evil for good.' C21's anger at full speed (counter-example, medium). Abigail intercepts him with food and with the Architecture of Peace in its exact form — the objective changed from who is right to what repair looks like, and one thing conceded early and out loud: 'On me, my lord, on me be the iniquity; and please let your handmaid speak in your ears.' She names what David is about to lose — 'that this shall be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself.' And David hears it: 'Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, that have kept me this day from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.' Non-Retaliation restored by someone else's wisdom. C15 and C16: 'your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.'

entries.pericope: As his share is who goes down to the battle, so shall his share be who tarries by the baggage: they shall share alike
entries.connection: Two hundred of David's men 'were so faint that they could not follow,' and stayed at the brook. After the victory, some of the fighters — 'wicked men and base fellows' — refuse them a share. David overrules them: 'You shall not do so, my brothers, with that which Yahweh has given to us… For as his share is who goes down to the battle, so shall his share be who tarries by the baggage: they shall share alike.' The spoil treated as a gift rather than a wage, and the weakest not penalised for their weakness. C16 and C13. 'He made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel to this day.'

entries.pericope: When the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead heard concerning him that which the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose, and went all night, and took the body of Saul
entries.connection: Saul's body hangs on the wall of a Philistine city. The men of Jabesh Gilead — whom Saul had rescued at the start of his reign (11:1-11) — 'arose, and went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth Shan… and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fasted seven days.' A debt remembered years later, paid to a king who could no longer reward anyone, at the risk of their lives. Unobligated Loyalty after defeat and death (medium). C13 and C16.
